messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mele’s life broke open on a Tuesday afternoon in the surgical waiting room of a county hospital. She was fifty-three then, still married, still an architect who believed in clean lines and sound structures. Her younger brother, Mana, had been airlifted in after a construction collapse on a site he was supervising. She sat for eleven hours in that room—fluorescent lights, the antiseptic smell that clung to every surface, the incomprehensible chatter of a dozen languages over the intercom, none of it making sense, none of it telling her whether he was alive. When a doctor finally came out, the words barely registered: massive internal injuries, sepsis, they had done what they could. Mana died the next morning. In the months that followed, Mele found she could not drive past that hospital without her chest tightening and her hands going numb on the wheel. The smell alone—rubbing alcohol, bleach, the sharp chemical ghost of a hallway—was enough to make her pull over and retch. She began taking longer routes to avoid the neighborhood entirely. When a routine physical was scheduled at her own clinic, she cancelled it three times before the receptionist stopped calling. She told herself it was practical, that she was busy, that architects don't have time for checkups. But what she really felt was that if she walked into that room, if she smelled that air again, she would lose control completely, and everyone would see it.

What frightened her most was the certainty that others could see what had happened just by looking at her. She had come to believe that the trauma was written on her face, in her posture, in the way she moved through a room. When colleagues at the firm spoke to her, she felt exposed, as though they were studying her for cracks. She stopped accepting invitations to dinner or coffee with friends because she was sure they were talking about her afterward, dissecting her like a failed blueprint. Nothing felt meaningful anymore. The projects that had once excited her—a library renovation, a community health center—now seemed hollow, exercises in arranging empty space. She had lost her faith in people, in the idea that effort or love or vigilance could protect anyone. The world, she was certain, was a place where the worst thing could happen without warning, and no one would tell you until it was too late.

The more she avoided, the more the world contracted. She started running at dawn, pushing herself until her lungs burned and her legs trembled, because the exhaustion was the only thing that quieted her mind. But the exercise itself became another kind of problem: after a punishing ten-mile run, she would collapse on her kitchen floor, and the silence that followed was filled with the same hospital sounds—the intercom, the chatter, the smell that seemed to have followed her home. She began to notice the smell everywhere: in a hand sanitizer dispenser at the grocery store, in a cleaning product her neighbor used, in the faint chemical residue on her own hands after she washed them. Each time, the same surge of panic, the same certainty that she was back in that waiting room, that Mana was still dying, that she had never actually left. The smell became a trigger she could not outrun, and the running itself—the compulsive, punishing miles—became a way of trying to escape something that was already inside her.

She has not seen her closest friends in over two years. She turned down a partnership track at the firm because she could not face the meetings, the handshakes, the crowded conference rooms where people might look at her and know. What finally brought her to seek help was a simple thing: she could no longer walk into a pharmacy. The antiseptic smell hit her at the door, and she stood frozen on the sidewalk, unable to go in for the aspirin she needed for a headache that had lasted three days. She is terrified that she will never feel safe again, that the world has become a minefield of triggers she cannot map or avoid. But she is also, somewhere underneath, hoping that a structure can be rebuilt—that there is a way to live without the smell, without the running, without the certainty that everyone can see what she carries.
